engine.summary: Scheduling: orders jobs on identical machines by a dispatching rule, searches job-shop schedules (each job a sequence of operations on machines) with a genetic algorithm, and checks a schedule against its problem's rules.

surfaces.name: u-schedule
surfaces.note: The crate is a framework: resource and activity models, dispatching rules, a GA encoding, constraint programming and KPIs; the WebAssembly operations are request-level entry points over it.
surfaces.error_shape: Err(...) of the solver's error type for a model or setting it cannot run.

surfaces.name: @iyulab/u-schedule
surfaces.note: Objects in and out, typed in the .d.ts (ScheduleInput, JobShopInput, JobShopCheckInput and their outputs). Bundler and Node targets; no bundler-less browser build.
surfaces.error_shape: A thrown Error whose code property is the code, with the fields (parameter, index, min, max, got, expected, ...) as its other properties.

errors.shape: A refusal carries a stable snake_case 'code' and the fields listed for that code; the checker reports violations in the same vocabulary as data, not as an error.

source.catalog: code_catalog in src/wasm.rs, built from the Code table refusals are made from and one example of every job-shop violation; published as codes() in WebAssembly. What each code means is tabled in README.md, which a test holds equal to the catalog.

operations.summary: Orders jobs on one or more identical machines by a dispatching rule (SPT, LPT, EDD, FCFS, CR, WSPT, MST, S/RO, ATC, LWKR, MWKR or PRIORITY), honouring release times, and reports each job's start and end, the makespan, the total tardiness and each machine's busy time and utilization.

checks.claim: Every rule on one to three machines returns each job once, no earlier than its release, for its processing time, with no two jobs at once on a machine; makespan, total tardiness, per-job tardiness, busy time and utilization equal the figures the entries add up to.
checks.reference: the definition of a feasible dispatching schedule and its figures
checks.method: 13 rules x 1-3 machines x 3 seeded eight-job shops, recomputed from the entries

checks.claim: On one machine with every job ready at 0, SPT minimises total completion time, WSPT total weighted completion time and EDD maximum lateness, against every order of six jobs.
checks.reference: Smith (1956), Jackson (1955): the optimality of SPT, WSPT and EDD
checks.method: five seeded six-job shops, 720 orders each

checks.claim: The unit of time does not change a schedule: scaling every time by 10, 1e3 or 1e5 gives the same order on the same machines, the starts scaled.
checks.reference: a schedule is unchanged by a change of unit
checks.method: 13 rules x 1-2 machines x 3 seeds x 3 scales

limits: Times are rounded to whole milliseconds (documented), so the unit check scales up only.
Rules other than SPT, WSPT and EDD are checked for feasibility and unit invariance, not for optimality of an objective.

operations.summary: A job-shop schedule found by a genetic algorithm over operation sequences, with optional machine alternatives, release times, due dates, transport times between machines and a weight on tardiness; reports every operation's machine and times, each job's completion and tardiness, the makespan and why the search stopped.

effects.note: The search draws from ga_config.seed when it is given and from fresh entropy when it is not.

determinism.note: The worst case, a search without ga_config.seed.

output_provenance.note: Whether the search ran its max_generations or stalled first, and how its best fitness moved.

checks.claim: On three jobs of three operations the makespan is never below the best of all 1,680 semi-active schedules and the search reaches it; the schedule's entries are feasible by an independent recomputation and the checker accepts them.
checks.reference: brute-force enumeration of all operation orders (the optimum by definition)
checks.method: six seeded shops, every order of the operations tried

checks.claim: Times scaled by 1e3 and 1e5 reach the optimum of the scaled shop.
checks.reference: a schedule is unchanged by a change of unit
checks.method: three seeded shops at two scales

limits: Optimality is only checked where it can be enumerated (three jobs of three operations); schedule quality has not been compared against best-known makespans of standard instances (Taillard, Lawrence).
Feasibility of a returned schedule is checkable with check_jobshop.

operations.summary: Whether a schedule keeps its job-shop problem, read as solve_jobshop reads it: each step of each job placed once, on a machine it can run on, for its processing time, after the step ahead of it and the job's release, no two steps on one machine at once, and the reported makespan equal to the latest end; lists every rule broken.

checks.claim: The checker accepts every schedule the solver returns, and a schedule that is not the solver's one names each way it breaks the problem.
checks.reference: the definition of a feasible job-shop schedule
checks.method: solver answers on six seeded shops checked; a broken schedule built per violation kind

limits: Each violation kind is covered by the unit test a_broken_schedule_names_each_violation; the oracle test covers only acceptance of the solver's own answers.

operations.summary: A better order for the same dispatching: a biased random-key genetic algorithm gives each operation a key and the dispatcher decodes each set of keys (the job whose next operation has the lower key first), so every schedule considered is one run_schedule could build; returns the better of the best keyed schedule and config.rule's own -- never worse than run_schedule -- with its cost ((1 - w) makespan + w total tardiness), the rule's cost, the generations run and why it stopped.

effects.note: The search draws from search.seed when it is given and from fresh entropy when it is not, and stops at search.time_limit_ms when one is given.

determinism.note: The worst case, a search without search.seed.

cases.note: How many generations run before the deadline depends on machine speed; with the same seed they are the same generations.

output_provenance.note: Whether the search ran its generations, stalled or hit the deadline, and how much it gained over the rule alone.

checks.claim: The searched schedule is feasible, its cost is (1 - w) x makespan + w x total tardiness of its entries, dispatching_cost is the rule's own schedule's cost, and the cost is never above it.
checks.reference: the definition of the cost the operation documents; the rule's schedule as the baseline
checks.method: four rule/machine/weight combinations x 3 seeded eight-job shops

limits: Schedule quality has not been compared against best-known solutions of standard instances.

operations.summary: The dispatching rules run_schedule takes and, for each, the config settings it reads; a request giving any other setting with that rule is refused.

limits: No independent reference: a unit test holds the catalog equal to the rules run_schedule accepts, which is a consistency check of the crate with itself.
